title: The Silk Road
passages: The Silk Road was not one single road but a web of trails that linked China with lands far to the west. Its story often begins around 138 BCE, when the Han DYNASTY sent an AMBASSADOR named Zhang Qian on a long journey to seek allies. He returned years later with news of distant kingdoms, fine horses and busy markets. By about 130 BCE, traders were moving goods along these routes regularly. The name itself is much newer. A German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, coined it in 1877, inspired by the shimmering Chinese silk that buyers in Rome prized so highly.

The routes stretched more than 4,000 miles, about 6,400 kilometers, from Chang'an in China to the Mediterranean Sea. Few travelers covered the whole distance. Instead, goods passed from city to city. CARAVANS of camels rested at Dunhuang, a desert OASIS famous for its painted caves, then pushed on to Kashgar, where merchants from many lands met in a lively bazaar. Farther west lay Samarkand and Bukhara, wealthy cities where Persian, Turkic and Chinese traders bargained side by side. Beyond them waited Baghdad and Constantinople. Along the way, people swapped not only silk and spices but also stories, music and new ideas.
